name: Saul
lede: Saul is a dark, grey-green name whose origin the books do not record; the only Sauls they discuss are people, among them the Bible's first king of Israel.

sections.title: A name with no recorded color
sections.body:
None of the color books we hold explains Saul as a color word [1][2]. Searching them turns up the name only as a person: an author's name in a bibliography, a novelist quoted in a dictionary of idioms, and the biblical king [1][2][3]. That is an honest gap, and we leave the origin undocumented rather than guess one.

The swatch is a deep grey-green, a little greyer than [[forest-green]] and darker than [[sage]]. Its name gives no hint of that, which is why the page below leans on measurement rather than history.

sections.title: The king in the books
sections.body:
The one color link the books offer is old and indirect. A dictionary of colour explains that scarlet was the dress of people of importance in the Bible, and gives Saul's clothing in 2 Samuel as the example, so that scarlet came to signal rank [2]. Pastoureau mentions Saul in a different way, among biblical figures such as Esau and Caiaphas whom medieval imagery tied to red and to unhappy fates [3]. Both uses point to red, not to grey-green, so neither explains this swatch [2][3].

If a paint maker or a catalogue once chose the name for this color, no source here says so [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, 399 contain this color as a large enough patch (about 1.7 per cent), as photographed [4]. It is about 5 times more common in Post-Impressionist paintings than in the archive as a whole, and about 10 times more common in the work of Paul Cezanne and Claude Monet than average [4]. Its share peaks in the 1440s and again in the 1900s [4]. These are photographs of varnished, aged paintings, so the color is as photographed, not as painted.

questions.q: What do the color books say about where the color name Saul comes from?
choices: It is named for the Bible's first king
Nothing: no source records its origin
It is a Victorian dye name
questions.answer: Nothing: no source records its origin
